extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (applicants/attorneys)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating obviousness (35 U.S.C. 103) in genus–species and chemical compound cases, including how to make fact-findings, analyze structural similarity, predictability, and consider applicant rebuttal evidence. Primarily directed to examiners assessing prima facie obviousness and applicants responding to rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham v. John Deere factors
rubrics_metrics.description: To make out a case of obviousness, one must: (A) determine the scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain the differences between the prior art and the claims in issue; (C) determine the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (D) evaluate any evidence of secondary considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a prima facie case is established, the burden shifts to applicant to come forward with rebuttal evidence or argument. Office personnel should evaluate the totality of the facts and all of the evidence to determine whether they support a conclusion that the claimed invention would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should determine the scope and content of the relevant prior art; each reference must qualify as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 102 and should be analogous art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before answering Graham's 'content' inquiry, it must be known whether a patent or publication is in the prior art under 35 U.S.C. § 102. See MPEP § 2141.01(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings for prior art genus — structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus, make findings as to the structure of the disclosed prior art genus and that of any expressly described species or subgenus within the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly identify the genus structure and any species/subgenus described; use these structural findings when comparing to the claimed species or subgenus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings for prior art genus — properties and utilities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus, make findings as to any physical or chemical properties and utilities disclosed for the genus, any suggested limitations on the usefulness of the genus, and any problems alleged to be addressed by the genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties/utilities disclosed in the reference provide motivation for selection; lack of useful properties weighs against a finding of motivation to make related compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings for prior art genus — predictability
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus, make findings as to the predictability of the technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Predictability affects whether structural similarity gives rise to an expectation of similar properties; unpredictable technologies reduce the force of structural similarity for obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Findings for prior art genus — number of species encompassed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus, make findings as to the number of species encompassed by the genus taking into consideration all of the variables possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider total circumstances (e.g., limited number of members, limited variations) — a very small, tightly defined genus may effectively disclose each member and support anticipation or obviousness in some cases; size alone is not determinative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ascertain differences between closest disclosed prior art species and claimed species
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and compare the closest disclosed prior art species or subgenus of record to the claimed species or subgenus to determine the differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make explicit findings on similarities and differences including findings relating to similarity of structure, properties, and utilities; the question is whether the claimed invention as a whole would have been obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the art
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the prior art from the standpoint of the hypothetical person having ordinary skill in the art at the time the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The level of skill is important for objectivity in the obviousness inquiry; facts of record pertaining to level of skill often are found within the prior art reference but additional applicant evidence should be evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determine whether a person of ordinary skill would be motivated to select the claimed species (motivation/suggestion)
rubrics_metrics.description: In light of findings relating to the Graham factors, determine whether it would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill to make the claimed invention as a whole, i.e., to select the claimed species or subgenus from the disclosed prior art genus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider all relevant prior art teachings, focusing on categories such as size of genus, express teachings, structural similarity, similar properties/uses, predictability of technology, and any other teachings; make explicit why the prior art would have motivated selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the size of the genus
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the size of the prior art genus when assessing motivation to select a claimed species from it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Size alone cannot support an obviousness rejection; however, a genus may be so small that, in light of total circumstances (limited variations, unchanging nucleus, etc.), it would effectively anticipate or render obvious a claimed species (see In re Petering and related cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider express teachings in the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art reference expressly teaches a particular reason to select the claimed species or subgenus, point out the express disclosure and explain why it would have been obvious to select the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An express teaching may be a statement such as an art-recognized equivalence or a reference specifically referring to another reference; cite and explain express teachings (e.g., Merck v. Biocraft).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of structural similarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider any teachings of a 'typical,' 'preferred,' or 'optimum' species within the disclosed genus and whether such species are structurally similar to the claimed species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structurally similar exemplary species may provide a reason to choose the claimed species based on expectation of similar properties; analyze number of variables to be selected/modified and significance of differences (including conservative substitutions in biotech/chemistry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider teachings of similar properties or uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider the properties and utilities of structurally similar prior art species or subgenus, because properties/utilities provide real world motivation to make related species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claimed and prior art species share any useful property, that generally motivates selection; conversely, lack of a disclosed useful property weighs against motivation. Very close structural similarity plus similar utilities can create a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider predictability of the technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider how predictable the technology is when assessing whether structural similarity provides a reasonable expectation of similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the technology is unpredictable, structurally similar species are less likely to render a claimed species obvious; obviousness requires only a reasonable expectation of success, not absolute predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider any other teachings to support selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond common categories, consider the totality of the evidence and any other relevant teachings sufficient to support selection of the species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The listed categories (size, express teaching, structural similarity, properties, predictability) are common but not exclusive; in unusual cases other teachings may be relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make express fact-findings supporting or refuting a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: Based on the evidence as a whole, make express fact-findings relating to the Graham factors and articulate what teachings or suggestions in the prior art would have motivated one of ordinary skill to select the claimed species or subgenus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After articulating fact-findings, determine whether these findings, considered as a whole, support a prima facie case of obviousness; cite appropriate case law where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie obviousness from close structural similarity (chemical compounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be made when chemical compounds have very close structural similarities and similar utilities; the motivation is the expectation that compounds similar in structure will have similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze structural and functional similarity together; use precedent (e.g., In re Payne, In re Dillon, In re Papesch) to assess whether similarity and shared utilities create motivation to make the claimed compound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat homology and isomerism as facts to be weighed with other evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Homologs, isomers, stereoisomers, and adjacent homologs are generally of sufficiently close structural similarity to create a presumed expectation of similar properties, but these facts must be considered with all other relevant facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate homology/isomerism automatically with prima facie obviousness; view claimed invention and prior art as a whole (see cases where homologs were and were not held prima facie obvious).

rubrics_metrics.name: True homologous/isomeric relationship not controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art structures do not have to be true homologs or isomers to render structurally similar compounds prima facie obvious; non-homologous but closely similar structures can be sufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate structural similarity and properties rather than relying solely on formal homolog/isomer labels (see In re Payne, In re Dillon, In re Mayne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence or absence of prior art method of making the claimed compound
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence—or absence—of a suitably operative, obvious process for making a composition of matter may have an ultimate bearing on whether that composition is obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prior art fails to disclose or render obvious a method for making the claimed compound at the relevant time, it may preclude concluding the compound is in the possession of the public and may overcome a presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of obviousness can be overcome by lack of reasonable expectation of similar properties
rubrics_metrics.description: The presumption of obviousness based on structural similarity may be overcome where there is evidence showing there is no reasonable expectation of similar properties in structurally similar compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence demonstrating unpredictability in the pertinent art area or lack of expectation of similar properties (e.g., In re May, In re Schechter) can rebut a prima facie case.

rubrics_metrics.name: If prior art compounds have no utility or only utility as intermediates, may not be prima facie obvious
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior art does not teach any specific or significant utility for disclosed compounds, or teaches them only as intermediates, the prior art is unlikely to render structurally similar claims prima facie obvious absent a reason to make such compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the reference teaches usefulness of the compounds; intermediates not known to have relevant utility weigh against motivation to select related compounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case rebuttable by evidence of superior or unexpected results
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness based on structural similarity is rebuttable by proof that the claimed compounds possess unexpectedly advantageous or superior properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal must be based on evidence (comparative data, affidavits); mere recognition of a benefit by the patentee is not sufficient if the prior art compound actually possessed the benefit. See MPEP § 716.02 and cases (Papesch, Wiechert, Dillon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and requirements of rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, failure of others), evidence of unexpected improved properties, copying by others, evidence about the state of the art, level of skill in the art, and beliefs of those skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may be presented in the specification, by counsel, or via affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132, but arguments of counsel cannot take the place of factually supported objective evidence. Consider all rebuttal arguments and evidence presented by applicants; evaluate the factual substance of declarations and data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden shifting upon establishment of a prima facie case
rubrics_metrics.description: If a prima facie case of obviousness is established, the burden shifts to the applicant to come forward with rebuttal arguments and/or evidence to overcome the prima facie case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may submit evidence in the specification, affidavits/declarations, or arguments, but evidence must be factual and supported; evaluate such rebuttal in light of the Graham factors and totality of the record.
